title: Routine maintenance
summary: Daily checks before you start, keeping to the service schedule, laying the engine up for winter and bringing it back, and the spares and tools to carry.

lessons.title: Daily pre-start checks
lessons.intro: WOBBLE is a widely used memory aid for the checks before and just after starting: Water, Oil, Belts, Bilges, Leaks and levels, and Exhaust. Doing them in the same order every time makes it hard to miss one, and finds problems while you are still safely tied up. The Checks tab has the same list to tick off.

diagram.caption: The WOBBLE order: five checks with the engine off, the final safety checks, then the exhaust once it is running.
diagram.description: A flow diagram of the WOBBLE checks in seven stages: water (coolant, seacock and strainer), oil, belts, bilges, leaks and levels, the final checks before starting, and, with the engine running, the exhaust.

lessons.caution: Do the hands-on checks with the engine stopped and unable to start. Once it is running, observe only and keep clear of belts, pulleys and the shaft.

steps.title: W: Water
steps.text: With the engine cold, check the freshwater coolant level in the header tank or expansion bottle; never open a hot pressure cap. Check the raw-water seacock is open and the strainer is clear, with its lid seated and sealed. A keel-cooled engine has no raw-water seacock for cooling, but may have one for its exhaust.

steps.title: O: Oil
steps.text: Check the engine oil on the dipstick and, if your gearbox has one, the gearbox oil. Look at the oil as well as the level: milky, frothy or fuel-smelling oil means something is getting into it. Do not start the engine; get advice.

steps.title: B: Belts
steps.text: Look over the alternator and pump drive belts for wear, cracking or fraying. Belt tension should be as your engine handbook specifies. Make sure nothing loose is lying near belts or pulleys.

steps.title: B: Bilges
steps.text: Look under the engine and in the bilge. Standing water, oil or fuel tells you something is leaking, and where to look first. Check that no water is coming in anywhere else either.

steps.title: L: Leaks and levels
steps.text: Make sure there is enough fuel for the trip with a good reserve and the fuel valve is open. Look for drips or weeping at seacocks, hoses and fittings, and over the exhaust hose for damage. Check the batteries, their connections and that the isolator is set for starting.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.text: Ventilate the engine space and make sure the air intake is clear. Where it is safe and practicable, check that no lines, fenders or people in the water are near the propeller. Put the gear lever in neutral and check the stop control works and is returned to the run position.

steps.title: E: Exhaust, once running
steps.text: Within a few seconds of starting, cooling water should come from a wet exhaust; if it does not, stop the engine. Check that the oil pressure and charging lights have gone out, and listen and look for unusual noise, vibration, belt squeal or smoke. Once warm, check the temperature is normal and look again for leaks without reaching near moving parts. Let the engine warm gently before asking for full power.

lessons.reviewNote: S15: the pre-start checks include water ingress, the air intake and engine space ventilation, the exhaust condition, and a propeller-clear check where safe and practicable. Revised in content 1.2 (owner request): now follows the WOBBLE memory aid, with the same checks as the pre-start and post-start checklists. Please approve.

lessons.title: Service intervals and records
lessons.intro: Engines last longest when they are serviced on time. Your handbook contains a schedule of jobs to do at set intervals, and a simple log makes it easy to keep to it.

steps.title: Running hours and time
steps.text: Most service jobs are due after a number of running hours, shown on the engine hour meter where one is fitted or kept in a written operating log where it is not, or after a period of time, whichever comes first. Boats used little still need servicing by time.

steps.title: Typical owner jobs
steps.text: Changing the engine oil and filter, fuel filters, the raw water impeller and the air filter; checking and renewing belts; checking anodes; and renewing coolant. Your handbook says which apply to your engine and how often.

steps.title: Specialist jobs
steps.text: Some jobs, such as checking valve clearances, servicing injectors or checking engine alignment, need special tools or skills. The handbook may say these should be done by a qualified engineer.

steps.title: Keep a log
steps.text: Write down each job with the date and engine hours, and the parts used. A log shows what is due next, helps an engineer find faults, and is valuable when you sell the boat.

steps.title: Use the right parts
steps.text: Fit filters, impellers and belts that match your engine's specification, and use the oil and coolant the handbook specifies. Note part numbers in your log so ordering spares is easy.

lessons.reviewNote: S19: running hours now come from the hour meter where fitted, otherwise from a documented operating log. Please approve.

lessons.title: Winterising and recommissioning
lessons.intro: An engine left unused for months can suffer from frost, corrosion and stale fuel. Laying it up properly in autumn, and bringing it back carefully in spring, prevents most early-season problems.
lessons.caution: Antifreeze is poisonous to people and animals. Store it securely and do not let it go into the water; follow local rules on disposal.

steps.title: Change the oil before lay-up
steps.text: Old oil contains acids that attack the engine while it stands. Changing the oil and filter before lay-up leaves the engine protected by clean oil all winter.

steps.title: Protect against frost
steps.text: Water left in the raw water circuit can freeze and crack the pump, heat exchanger or exhaust parts. How to protect it, whether by draining or by running a suitable antifreeze through it, and which type of antifreeze to use, depends on your engine and climate: follow the engine maker's method exactly. Check the coolant gives enough frost protection.

steps.title: Fuel
steps.text: Drain any water from the filter bowl. Aim to leave clean, dry fuel and keep water out. Whether to leave the tank full or low over winter depends on your fuel, how quickly you use it and where the boat is stored; follow your engine maker's and fuel supplier's advice, including on additives.

steps.title: Impeller and openings
steps.text: Some owners remove the impeller for the winter so its vanes do not take a set; this is optional and depends on the pump and the handbook. If you block the air intake or exhaust outlet against damp, put a clear note on the engine controls so the blanks are removed before starting.

steps.title: Batteries
steps.text: Keep batteries charged over winter, either with a suitable charger or by charging them regularly. A flat battery left in the cold can be permanently damaged.

steps.title: Recommissioning
steps.text: Remove any blanks and notes, refit the impeller, and check hoses, clips, belts and all fluid levels. Open the seacocks once afloat and check every through-hull and the stern seal for leaks. Start the engine, check for water from the exhaust and watch for leaks as it warms up.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 29, revise (S18): raw water circuit protection, antifreeze type and draining method now follow the engine maker; full tanks and impeller removal are no longer presented as universal. Please approve.

lessons.title: Spares and tool kit
lessons.intro: Most engine problems at sea can be fixed with a modest kit of spares and tools, as long as they are on board, fit your engine, and you know where they are.

steps.title: Essential spares
steps.text: Fuel filter elements with their seals, a raw water impeller with its cover gasket, a drive belt, engine oil and an oil filter, coolant, a selection of hose clips, and fuses for the engine panel.

steps.title: Useful extras
steps.text: A length of hose matching your cooling hoses, self-amalgamating tape for temporary repairs, spare bulbs for the panel, and stern gland packing or grease if your gland uses it.

steps.title: Tools
steps.text: Spanners and sockets in the sizes your engine uses, screwdrivers, a filter wrench, a tool for removing the impeller, an oil extraction pump, a multimeter and a good torch. Check each fits before you need it.

steps.title: Consumables
steps.text: Rags, gloves, a container for fuel and oil, absorbent pads for spills and a bag for oily waste.

steps.title: Information
steps.text: Keep the engine handbook on board, with your log, part numbers and labelled photos of the engine. A small notebook of what worked last time is surprisingly useful.

steps.title: Stow it well
steps.text: Keep spares dry and labelled, and know where each one is. A spare you cannot find in a seaway is no help.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to look in the bilge under the engine before starting?
options: Fresh oil, fuel or coolant there points to a leak and where to look
To check that the propeller is clear of weed and rope
To check the fuel level through the fuel tank's inspection hatch
To check the battery charge by looking at its indicator
questions.explanation: Fluids that leak from the engine collect in the bilge beneath it. Spotting them before starting lets you trace a leak while it is still minor.

questions.prompt: What should you check immediately after the engine starts?
options: That the warning lights are out and water is coming from the exhaust
That the fuel gauge shows the tank is completely full
That the stern gland is dripping fast enough to cool it
That the batteries have been switched off to save charge
questions.explanation: These two checks confirm that the oil pressure, charging and raw water cooling are all working before you rely on the engine.

questions.prompt: Why is it worth doing your pre-start checks in the same order every time?
options: A fixed routine makes it much harder to miss a check
The engine will not start if the order changes
The checks must be done in the order printed on the panel
It makes the engine warm up faster
questions.explanation: Routine turns the checks into a habit, so a missing step feels wrong. Changing the order each time makes it easy to skip something.

questions.prompt: Why should you let the engine warm gently before using full power?
options: Oil flows and protects best once warm, and parts expand evenly
Cold diesel is too thick for the injection pump at high revs
The gearbox will not engage properly until its oil is warm
The alternator needs time to recharge the battery before taking load
questions.explanation: Cold oil is thick and reaches bearings more slowly, and a cold engine has tighter clearances in some places. A gentle warm-up reduces wear.

questions.prompt: Before starting, you see a thin film of oil and a little coolant in the bilge that was not there yesterday. What should you do?
options: Find the source before relying on the engine, starting with levels and hoses
Pump the bilge out over the side and carry on as planned
Start the engine and run it hard for a while to see whether the leak gets worse
Top up the oil and coolant, then ignore it unless it gets worse
questions.explanation: New fluid in the bilge means something has changed. Checking levels and tracing the leak first can prevent an engine failure later. Running the engine hard to see whether a leak gets worse can turn a small fault into a failure or a fire, and oily water must not be pumped overboard.

questions.prompt: You have started the engine and are about to engage gear for the first time. Where it is safe and practicable, what should you check first?
options: That the propeller is clear of lines and people
That the engine has reached full working temperature
That the stern gland is dripping steadily
That the fuel tank is more than half full
questions.explanation: A line or fender caught round the propeller can stall the engine and damage the shaft, and anyone in the water near it is in danger. Look before you engage gear.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.1 (S15): the propeller-clear pre-start check. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Where should you find the service schedule for your engine?
options: In the engine manufacturer's handbook
On the engine's identification plate
On the battery label
In the boat's insurance policy documents
questions.explanation: The handbook lists each service job and when it is due. Intervals vary between engines, so the handbook is the reference.

questions.prompt: A service is due 'by running hours or by time, whichever comes first'. Your engine has done few hours this year. What does this mean?
options: The service is still due once the time limit is reached
The service can wait until the running hours are reached
The service is no longer needed
The service is due only once both limits have been reached
questions.explanation: Oil ages, rubber parts perish and corrosion continues even when the engine is not used. That is why there is a time limit as well as an hours limit.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to keep a written log of engine maintenance?
options: It shows what is due next and helps an engineer track down faults
It is required by law for every leisure boat with an inboard engine
It replaces the need to keep the engine handbook on board
It makes the engine use noticeably less fuel each season
questions.explanation: A log of dates, hours and parts tells you when jobs are due and gives an engineer a history to work from. It also adds value when you sell the boat.

questions.prompt: Which of these jobs is normally one for a qualified engineer rather than the owner?
options: Servicing the injectors
Changing the engine oil
Cleaning the raw water strainer
Draining water from the fuel filter bowl
questions.explanation: Injectors need specialist equipment to test and set them. The other jobs are routine owner maintenance.

questions.prompt: Where one is fitted, what shows how many running hours the engine has done?
options: The engine hour meter
The tachometer (rev counter)
The service sticker on the oil filter
The temperature gauge
questions.explanation: The hour meter records how long the engine has run, and many service intervals are based on it. Not every engine has one; without it, keep a written log of running time.
questions.reviewNote: Audit note 28, revise (S19): the question now says 'where one is fitted', and the explanation covers keeping a log on engines without a meter. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Why is the engine oil usually changed before the winter lay-up rather than in spring?
options: So the engine is not left standing all winter in acidic used oil
Because new oil can freeze in the bottle if it is left until spring
So the oil has the winter to settle before the first start
So the engine turns over faster on the first spring start
questions.explanation: Used oil contains acids from combustion. Leaving it in the engine for months encourages corrosion, so fresh oil goes in before lay-up.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of leaving sea water in the raw water circuit in a hard frost?
options: It can freeze and crack the pump, heat exchanger or other parts
It breeds diesel bug, which then spreads into the fuel
It slowly drains the batteries through the engine
It makes the engine oil too thick to pump in spring
questions.explanation: Water expands when it freezes, and the force can split castings and pipes. Handbooks explain whether to drain the circuit or fill it with antifreeze.

questions.prompt: You block the exhaust outlet and air intake for the winter. What else should you do?
options: Put a clear note on the engine controls to remove them before starting
Nothing, because the engine will push the blanks out as soon as it starts
Note it in a logbook that you keep at home
Paint over them so they stay watertight
questions.explanation: Starting with the intake or exhaust blocked can cause serious damage. A note on the controls makes sure whoever starts the engine next removes them.

questions.prompt: When recommissioning, why should you check the stern seal and through-hull fittings once the boat is afloat?
options: Out of the water nothing is pressing on them, so leaks cannot show
Hose clips loosen over winter and are easiest to tighten afloat
Through-hull fittings are checked by the insurer at each launch
Antifreeze left in them over winter has to be flushed out first
questions.explanation: Out of the water there is nothing to leak. Checking straight after launch catches a perished hose, a loose clip or a seal that needs attention before you leave.

questions.prompt: Why should batteries be kept charged over the winter?
options: A flat battery left in the cold can be permanently damaged
Charged batteries give off a little heat that keeps the engine warm
Charging keeps the alternator bearings from seizing
Charging keeps the stern gland's seal from drying out
questions.explanation: Many batteries are damaged if left discharged, and a flat battery is more likely to be harmed by frost. A suitable charger or regular charging prevents this.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an essential engine spare to carry on board?
options: A raw water impeller with its cover gasket
A complete spare cylinder head assembly and gasket
A spare crankshaft and set of bearings
A complete second gearbox, ready to fit
questions.explanation: Impellers wear out and fail without warning, and changing one is a common at-sea repair. Major engine parts are not practical spares.

questions.prompt: Why should you carry spare fuel filter elements?
options: Blocked fuel filters are a common reason for an engine stopping
Fuel filters need changing every time you go out
The engine will not start once a filter is a year old
Spare elements are needed to bleed the fuel system
questions.explanation: Rough weather can stir up dirt that blocks a filter quickly. A spare element and the tools to fit it can get the engine running again at sea.

questions.prompt: What is the point of checking that your spare belt and tools fit while you are in harbour?
options: So you know the repair is possible before you need to do it at sea
So the spares stay warm and supple until they are needed
Because spares slowly wear out if they are never used
Because the boat's warranty needs the spares to be tried
questions.explanation: A belt of the wrong size or a spanner that does not fit is only discovered when you try to use it. Trying in calm conditions avoids nasty surprises.

questions.prompt: Which of these is most useful for a temporary repair to a leaking cooling hose?
options: Self-amalgamating tape
Electrical insulating tape
Ordinary duct tape
Bathroom silicone sealant
questions.explanation: Self-amalgamating tape fuses to itself when stretched and wrapped, making a tight seal that can hold until the hose is replaced. Ordinary tapes and sealants do not hold against water pressure and heat.

questions.prompt: Why is it worth recording part numbers for your filters, impeller and belt in your log?
options: So you can order the right parts quickly and avoid ones that do not fit
Recording them is a legal requirement for all leisure boats
Once recorded, any make of filter can be used safely
The insurer needs them before it will cover the engine
questions.explanation: Similar-looking parts often differ in size, thread or rating. Having the exact numbers to hand means you get the right part first time, even from a chandler far from home.

questions.prompt: In the WOBBLE memory aid for engine checks, what do the letters stand for?
options: Water, Oil, Belts, Bilges, Leaks and levels, Exhaust
Water, Oil, Batteries, Bearings, Lights, Engine
Wiring, Oil, Belts, Batteries, Lubrication, Exhaust
Water, Oil, Bolts, Bilges, Lights, Electrics
questions.explanation: WOBBLE covers the coolant and raw water, oil, drive belts, bilges, leaks and fuel and battery levels, and finally the exhaust once the engine is running.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.2 (owner request): question on the pre/post-start checklists. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Which WOBBLE check is made with the engine running rather than before it starts?
options: Exhaust: cooling water coming out of the exhaust
Belts: wear, cracking and tension
Bilges: no water, oil or fuel under the engine
Oil: the level on the dipstick
questions.explanation: The E is the only check that needs the engine running: water from a wet exhaust shows the raw water pump is delivering. Belts, bilges and oil are checked with the engine off.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.2 (owner request): question on the pre/post-start checklists. Please approve.

questions.prompt: You start the engine and after several seconds no cooling water is coming out of the wet exhaust. What should you do?
options: Stop the engine and find the cause before running it again
Raise the revs to help the pump draw water through
Leave it at tickover and check again in ten minutes
Carry on, as the water will appear once the engine is warm
questions.explanation: With no water flow the engine and the wet exhaust are not being cooled, and the impeller is running dry. Raising the revs or leaving it running can damage the impeller, exhaust hose and silencer within a short time and overheat the engine.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.2 (owner request): question on the pre/post-start checklists. Please approve.

questions.prompt: During your pre-start checks the engine oil on the dipstick looks milky. What should you do?
options: Leave the engine off and get advice from a qualified engineer
Top it up with fresh oil and start as normal
Start the engine and run it hard to drive off the moisture
Change the oil filter and carry on with the trip
questions.explanation: Milky oil suggests water or coolant is mixing with it. Running the engine on contaminated oil can damage the bearings, and topping up or changing the filter hides the problem without finding where the water is coming from.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.2 (owner request): question on the pre/post-start checklists. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Shortly after starting, you realise the raw-water seacock was left closed. What should you do?
options: Stop the engine, open the seacock, and check the impeller and water flow before relying on the engine
Open the seacock with the engine running and carry on without further checks
Leave it closed until the engine has warmed up, then open it
Increase the revs so the pump can draw water past the closed seacock
questions.explanation: Running with the seacock closed lets the impeller run dry, which can damage its vanes within a short time, and leaves the wet exhaust uncooled. Carrying on without checking risks an overheated engine or a burnt exhaust hose later in the trip.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.2 (owner request): question on the pre/post-start checklists. Please approve. Please confirm the recommended response, including whether the impeller should always be inspected.

questions.prompt: Why should the freshwater coolant level be checked only with the engine cold?
options: A hot pressure cap can release scalding coolant when opened
Antifreeze loses its strength if it meets air while hot
The thermostat sticks open if the cap is removed when warm
The header tank empties itself while the engine is warm
questions.explanation: A warm cooling system is under pressure. Opening the cap lets the coolant boil and spray out, which can scald you. Wait until the engine is cold.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.2 (owner request): question on the pre/post-start checklists. Please approve.

questions.prompt: With the engine running and warm, you want to look again for leaks. How should you do it?
options: Look carefully, keeping hands, clothing and hair well clear of belts, pulleys and the shaft
Feel along the hoses near the belts by hand to find damp patches
Take off the belt guard so you can see behind the pulleys
Hold a rag against the drive belt to see whether it picks up oil
questions.explanation: With the engine running, a hand, sleeve or rag near a belt, pulley or shaft can be caught and pulled in, causing serious injury. Check by eye only; touch nothing near moving parts until the engine is stopped.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.2 (owner request): question on the pre/post-start checklists. Please approve.

questions.prompt: What should you check about the drive belts before starting?
options: That they show no wear, cracking or fraying, and are tensioned as the handbook specifies
That they are as tight as you can possibly make them
That they are slack enough to lift off the pulleys by hand
That they have been dressed with oil so they do not squeal
questions.explanation: A worn or wrongly tensioned belt can slip or break, stopping the raw water pump or alternator. Too tight a belt loads the bearings, and oil on a belt makes it slip; follow the handbook's tension.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.2 (owner request): question on the pre/post-start checklists. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Before starting the engine, where should the gear lever be?
options: In neutral
In ahead, so the boat moves off as soon as it starts
In astern, to hold the boat back against its lines
Anywhere, because the gearbox always disengages for starting
questions.explanation: Starting in gear can make the boat lurch into a pontoon, another boat or a person in the water, and can strain the lines. Some installations will not crank unless the lever is in neutral, but do not rely on that; check it every time.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.2 (owner request): question on the pre/post-start checklists. Please approve.
